bull_thesis:
The bull case is that Figma's shares were broken by plumbing rather than by business decay, and that the plumbing has a contractual end date eight trading days away. The franchise is genuinely healthy. Revenue was $333.4 million in the first quarter of 2026, up 46% from a year earlier, and that was the third consecutive quarter of acceleration (38% in the third quarter of 2025, 40% in the fourth, 46% in the first of 2026). Trailing-twelve-month revenue is $1.161 billion, up about 41%. Management then guided the second quarter to $348-350 million against a street carrying roughly $330 million, and raised the full-year guide by $55 million to $1.422-1.428 billion. Net dollar retention -- how much a given group of existing customers spends this year versus last -- climbed to 139%, its best reading in more than two years, and customers spending over $10,000 a year grew about 37% to 15,218. The company generated $88.6 million of free cash flow in the quarter, a 27% margin, and about $239 million over twelve months, against $1.638 billion of cash and short-term investments and only $56 million of debt -- roughly $1.58 billion of net cash, about $2.99 per share, and no financing risk of any kind.

At $22.94 the enterprise value (market value plus debt minus cash) is about $10.5 billion, roughly 7.4 times this year's guided revenue and about 6 times the $1.761 billion the street expects in 2027. For a business compounding in the mid-30s with a cash margin above 20%, that is a distressed price for a franchise that is not distressed.

The event is verified rather than assumed. Under the extended lock-up agreement entered on 30 August 2025 with holders of about 54.1% of the Class A shares, the final tranche of roughly 77.7 million shares releases at the open on the second trading day after the second-quarter 2026 earnings announcement, which the company confirmed on 15 July 2026 for Wednesday 5 August 2026. That makes Friday 7 August 2026 the date, and the lock-up terminates there. After it, no Figma share is contractually restricted and the overhang that has defined this stock since listing is gone for good. The bull argument is that the market has pre-positioned against exactly that date: 66.1 million shares are still sold short, about 27.75% of the tradable float, and crowded shorts placed against a known date have to cover into it. The stock has already shown what that looks like -- up 11.9% on 13 July 2026 and up 8.6% on 27 July 2026 with no company news attached to either move. Three large banks turned constructive within a month: Citigroup initiated Buy on 1 July 2026 (target trimmed to $35 on 24 July), Bank of America reinstated with Buy and $30 on 7 July, and Goldman Sachs carries Buy and $30, all arguing that artificial intelligence strengthens rather than threatens Figma's position. Fourteen covering firms average about $30.40. Findell Capital told the board publicly on 28 May 2026 that the company is significantly undervalued. The conditions this case needs: growth above roughly 35% at the 5 August print, gross margin stabilising near 79-80%, and the 7 August release absorbed without a sustained break of the June low.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that the verified event points the wrong way, that the positioning fuel has already been burned, and that the floor beneath the position is imaginary.

Start with direction. A forced-seller thesis pays when a known seller is about to be exhausted and the price is then free to rise. What actually happens on 7 August 2026 is the opposite in the near term: about 77.7 million shares are added to a tradable float of roughly 238 million -- a one-third increase in supply in a single step -- handed to venture funds that have already demonstrated they distribute in kind and price-blind. Index Ventures moved about 3.5 million shares out on 19 May 2026 and still holds roughly 53 million; the director and 10% owner Mamoon Hamid moved about 6.0 million out on 28 May 2026 and still holds 37.1 million. Those two alone control about 90 million shares. Nothing about the release exhausts supply thereafter: with the lock-up gone there is no restriction left, and stock-based compensation runs near half of revenue, manufacturing roughly 10% more shares every year regardless of any agreement -- weighted average shares went from 474.8 million to 523.5 million in a single year.

Then the positioning. The squeeze that is supposed to pay us is already being harvested. Short interest has fallen from 78.2 million shares a month ago to 66.1 million now, 27.75% of float and 2.9 days to cover, while the stock rallied about 38% off its June low. A new buyer today is buying the second half of a cover, not the first.

The business case is weaker than the growth headline. Gross margin fell from 91.5% to 79.4% in a single year because cost of revenue rose 253%, from $19.5 million to $68.7 million, as artificial-intelligence inference compute landed in the cost line -- and management did not frame that for investors in advance. On a generally-accepted-accounting-principles basis the company lost $142.4 million in the quarter and about $1.40 billion over twelve months. RBC downgraded to Sector Perform at a $22 target on exactly this margin pressure. Anthropic's launch of Claude Design at the end of April 2026 is the structural question the market is actually pricing: whether per-seat design software survives when the design step can be generated. The company's own answer -- rebranding at its June 2026 Config conference as an intelligent canvas and buying the Bud team on 7 July 2026 -- is a real pivot, but a pivot is an admission that the old ground is moving.

Finally, the price. The board file underwrote this at roughly $20.49 with a $17.50 floor. That floor has already been broken -- the shares traded to $16.60 in late June 2026 -- and the stock has since rallied about 38% off that low, so the buyer today is paying up for an event that has not happened yet. There is no deal price, no cash tender, no contingent payment right; net cash of $2.99 per share is nowhere near the market price and therefore backstops nothing. What confirms the bear: a second-quarter print at or below the $348 million guide, gross margin below 79%, or a sustained close under $16.60 in the two weeks after the release.
sop_bull:
Event-win value of about $30 per share. Figma reports a single operating segment, so the parts here are the operating franchise plus the balance sheet rather than separable divisions.

Operating business: if the 7 August 2026 release is absorbed, growth holds in the mid-30s and gross margin stabilises near 80%, the franchise earns roughly 8 to 8.5 times consensus 2027 revenue of $1.761 billion -- a discount to high-retention software peers that still respects the artificial-intelligence question -- which is about $14.1 to $15.0 billion of enterprise value, or roughly $26.70 to $28.30 per share on 528.4 million shares.

Balance-sheet overlay: $1.638 billion of cash and short-term investments less $56.2 million of total debt is $1.582 billion, about $2.99 per share, and it is genuinely surplus because the business already funds itself with about $239 million of trailing free cash flow. No pending distribution, no announced asset sale, no deal terms to layer on -- this is a clean two-part sum.

Sum: roughly $29.70 to $31.30, call it $30. This is corroborated independently rather than reverse-engineered: fourteen covering analysts average about $30.40, with Bank of America and Goldman Sachs both at $30 and Citigroup at $35. A short-covering overshoot above that is possible with 66.1 million shares still short, but overshoot is not value and is not carried here.
sop_bear:
Verified downside floor of about $16.50 per share, and it is a soft one.

Operating business: on a decelerating growth rate and a permanently lower gross margin, the franchise is worth about 3.5 to 4 times consensus 2027 revenue of $1.761 billion -- where unprofitable software with a contested end-market has repeatedly cleared -- which is $6.16 to $7.04 billion of enterprise value, or roughly $11.70 to $13.30 per share.

Balance-sheet overlay: net cash of $1.582 billion adds about $2.99 per share.

Sum: roughly $14.70 to $16.30. The tape has already tested this: the stock printed $16.60 in late June 2026, which broke the board file's $17.50 floor. Take $16.50 as the verified floor -- the intersection of the arithmetic and the tested low -- and be honest that it is a sentiment level, not a backstop. There is no deal price, no tender, no contingent payment right and no covenant forcing anything. The only hard asset value is the $2.99 per share of net cash, which does not bind anywhere near the current price. If the artificial-intelligence displacement case is right rather than merely feared, nothing stops the stock going through $16.50 to the low teens.
sop_breakdown:
Probability-weighted between the two outcomes, because there is no contractual payout to anchor to.

Win case $30: the operating franchise at about 8 to 8.5 times consensus 2027 revenue of $1.761 billion (roughly $27 per share) plus $2.99 per share of net cash.

Loss case $16.50: the same franchise at about 3.5 to 4 times that revenue (roughly $12.50 per share) plus the same $2.99 of net cash, ratified by the tested June 2026 low of $16.60.

We put the odds close to even -- call it 50/50 -- because the two forces genuinely offset. On one side, a one-third increase in tradable float on 7 August 2026 handed to price-blind distributors. On the other, 66.1 million shares still sold short into that same date. A straight 50/50 on the $29 board target and the $16.50 floor gives about $22.75; giving modest credit for the raised full-year guide and 139% net dollar retention lifts the base case to about $23.

The uncomfortable conclusion is that at $22.94 the stock is already trading at its probability-weighted value. The discount this idea was underwritten on has been paid out by a 38% rally off the June low, before the event fired.
risk_reward: About 0.9 to 1, which is not enough. From $22.94 the upside to the $29 event-win target is about +26% (+33% to the $30.40 analyst average); the downside to the verified $16.50 floor is about -28%, and that floor is sentiment rather than contract. The board file underwrote 2.85 to 1 at roughly $20.49 against a $17.50 floor. Both sides have moved against us: the entry is 12% higher and the floor is 6% lower, because $17.50 was broken in June 2026. Re-entry at or below $18.50 against the same $29 target restores roughly 5 to 1 -- that is the level worth waiting for, and the 7 August 2026 supply release is the mechanism most likely to deliver it.
catalyst_summary: The last contractual lock-up on Figma stock -- about 77.7 million shares, a third of the tradable float -- expires at the open on Friday 7 August 2026, two trading days after the 5 August second-quarter report; the overhang clears for good, but at $22.94 after a 38% rally and with the short book already 15% smaller than a month ago, the buyer is paid about 26% to the $29 target against 28% downside to a $16.50 floor that has already been broken once.
dated_milestone:
Friday 7 August 2026 -- the final extended lock-up tranche of approximately 77.7 million Class A shares is released at the commencement of trading on the second trading day after the second-quarter 2026 earnings announcement, and the extended lock-up period terminates. The earnings announcement itself is Wednesday 5 August 2026 after the United States close, with a call at 5 p.m. Eastern, confirmed by the company on 15 July 2026. The backstop date written into the agreement, 31 August 2026, will not be reached because the earnings trigger comes first.

Verified from the company's own disclosure rather than inferred. In an agreement entered on 30 August 2025 and disclosed on 3 September 2025, Figma bound holders of approximately 54.1% of its outstanding Class A common stock not to sell, pledge or hedge, releasing stock in four earnings-triggered steps: about 38.9 million shares (17.5%) after the third-quarter 2025 report, about 44.4 million (20%) after the full-year 2025 report, about 61.1 million (27.5%) after the first-quarter 2026 report, and the remainder -- about 77.7 million shares -- on the earlier of (i) the commencement of trading on the second trading day after the company announces earnings for the quarter ending 30 June 2026 and (ii) 31 August 2026. The extended lock-up period terminates on that final release. Figma announced on 15 July 2026 that second-quarter 2026 results are released after the United States close on Wednesday 5 August 2026, which puts the final release at the open on Friday 7 August 2026. The event is therefore dated, contractual, binding and inside the window. Two caveats travel with the status: the event releases supply rather than resolving value, and the three earlier tranches have already released, which is why officers and venture funds have been selling freely since May 2026. Re-verified 28 July 2026 against the company's earnings-date announcement and the lock-up disclosure; no slippage, no amendment, no change to the trigger.
forcing_function:
The catalyst is the pair of dates in the first week of August 2026.

On Wednesday 5 August the company reports the second quarter against its own guide of $348-350 million and a raised full-year range of $1.422-1.428 billion. That print settles the two live questions: is growth still above 35%, and has gross margin stopped falling from the 79.4% it reached in the first quarter of 2026.

Two trading days later, at the open on Friday 7 August, roughly 77.7 million shares come free and the extended lock-up agreement signed on 30 August 2025 terminates. That is the moment the last contractual restriction on Figma stock disappears.

It forces a re-rating in one of two directions and there is no third path. Either the release is absorbed and the short book -- still 66.1 million shares, 27.75% of the float -- has to cover into a franchise growing in the mid-30s at 6 times next year's revenue; or the venture funds distribute into a thin bid and the stock retests the $16.60 June low. The honest reading is that the second path is where the opportunity is: this event creates the entry, it does not pay the position.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market runs in both directions, and that symmetry is itself the reason to wait rather than to buy.

The street is wrong on demand. The tape has priced Figma as a business being deleted by artificial intelligence: down about 84% from the August 2025 peak of $142.92, at roughly 7.4 times this year's guided revenue and 6 times the 2027 consensus of $1.761 billion. The reported numbers do not support deletion. Revenue accelerated for three consecutive quarters to 46% growth in the first quarter of 2026, net dollar retention rose to 139%, customers above $10,000 of annual spend grew 37%, management guided the second quarter above the street and raised the full-year range by $55 million on artificial-intelligence monetisation, with roughly three-quarters of enterprise customers buying artificial-intelligence credits. A business being disintermediated does not have existing customers spending 39% more than they did a year ago. RBC's $22 target and the Hold ratings implicitly assume the transition destroys the model; the retention data says it is currently expanding it.

But the street is also wrong in our favour less than the board file assumed, in two specific places.

First, the bull consensus underweights the gross margin. Cost of revenue rose 253% year over year while revenue rose 46%, taking reported gross margin from 91.5% to 79.4% in twelve months. If inference compute keeps scaling with usage under the new credit-based pricing, the terminal margin is structurally lower than the revenue multiple being argued for -- the $30 targets are set on sales, not on the cash the business will actually keep.

Second, and more immediately, the market is not mispricing the lock-up; it is trading it. Short interest peaked and has already begun to unwind, from 78.2 million shares a month ago to 66.1 million now, while the stock rallied 38% off its June low. That is not an overlooked event; it is the most heavily traded fact about this stock, and our edge on timing is correspondingly small.

The genuine disagreement that survives: we think the post-release Figma -- with no contractual restriction left, a cleared overhang, $1.58 billion of net cash and mid-30s growth -- is worth roughly $30, and that the market will only concede that after it sees the 77.7 million shares absorbed. That is a view about late August, not about today.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is short, specific and about eight trading days away. It is a supply-and-sentiment problem, not a solvency one. There is no cash-burn hump, no debt maturity and no covenant: Figma holds $1.638 billion of cash and short-term investments against $56.2 million of debt and generated about $239 million of free cash flow over the last twelve months, so the company can survive any share price.

The position may not. Three things land on top of each other. First, the second-quarter print on 5 August 2026 carries a raised bar -- management guided $348-350 million against a street that was near $330 million, so an in-line quarter is now a disappointment, and the gross-margin line will be read harder than the revenue line. Second, at the open on 7 August about 77.7 million shares are released, roughly a third of the 238 million share float, to holders whose observed behaviour is to distribute in kind to limited partners without regard to price; Index Ventures did so on 19 May 2026 and Mamoon Hamid on 28 May 2026, and between them they still hold about 90 million shares. Third, the stock enters both events having already rallied about 38% off the $16.60 June low, which removes the cushion a washed-out price would have provided, and with the short book that would have to buy it back already 15% smaller than it was a month ago.

Beyond August, the slower grind is dilution and margin. Stock-based compensation near half of revenue adds roughly 10% to the share count every year -- a permanent supply of stock that no lock-up expiry fixes -- and the competitive question reopens with every product launch from a well-funded rival. The realistic bad path is not bankruptcy; it is a retest of $16.60 in the second half of August followed by months of range-bound trading while the venture distributions work through. That is precisely the window in which patient capital should be buying rather than holding through.
positioning_washout:
Forced-selling pressure is the entire thesis on this name, and for the first time it has a termination date rather than an open end.

The mechanical sellers are the pre-listing venture funds. They do not sell in the ordinary sense; they distribute shares in kind to their limited partners, who then liquidate at their own convenience and without reference to valuation. That flow is visible and dated: Index Ventures moved about 3.5 million shares out on 19 May 2026 and still holds roughly 53 million; Mamoon Hamid, a director and 10% owner, moved about 6.0 million out on 28 May 2026 and still holds 37.1 million. The May timing is not coincidence -- the third lock-up tranche of about 61.1 million shares released two trading days after the first-quarter 2026 report. The fourth and final tranche of about 77.7 million shares releases at the open on 7 August 2026, after which no Figma share is contractually restricted. Officer selling has run alongside it continuously, most recently the chief revenue officer on 14 July 2026 at $23.92.

On the other side sits the short book, and this is where the picture has changed. Short interest is 66.1 million shares, about 27.75% of the tradable float and 12.5% of shares outstanding, at 2.9 days to cover -- down from 78.2 million a month ago. Research desks were describing 35-42% of float in mid-July; the covering has already started. Both the 11.9% jump on 13 July 2026 and the 8.6% jump on 27 July 2026 came without company news, which is what forced covering looks like. The problem for a buyer today is that this is the fuel, and it is being burned before the event rather than by it.

The two flows collide in the same week, and that is why we are not sizing this before it. The clean version of this trade is to let the 77.7 million shares print, watch whether the June low holds, and buy the exhaustion rather than the anticipation. One structural caveat: because stock-based compensation runs near half of revenue and creates roughly 10% new shares annually, supply here is never fully exhausted -- the 7 August release ends the contractual overhang, not the dilution.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a real, dated, binding event on a better business than the tape says -- and it is still not a buy today, for reasons of price and direction rather than doubt.

Start with what is verified. The extended lock-up agreement of 30 August 2025 covers about 54.1% of the Class A shares and releases them in four earnings-triggered steps, the last of which -- roughly 77.7 million shares -- comes free at the open on the second trading day after the second-quarter 2026 report, which the company confirmed on 15 July 2026 for 5 August. That makes Friday 7 August 2026 the date, and the agreement terminates there. The event is hard, contractual and inside the window. It has not slipped and it has not been amended.

Now the three reasons that does not translate into capital this week.

Direction. A forced-seller thesis pays when a known seller is exhausted and the price is freed. This event first adds about a third to the tradable float, handing it to venture funds that have already demonstrated they distribute in kind and price-blind, and it leaves nothing behind to restrain them afterwards. The clearing is genuine but it arrives supply-first.

Positioning. The squeeze that was supposed to be our payment is already being collected by someone else. Short interest has fallen from 78.2 million shares to 66.1 million over the past month while the stock rose 38%. Two newsless double-digit up-days in July are the receipts. Buying now is buying the second half of a cover.

Price. The board file underwrote 2.85 to 1 at about $20.49 against a $17.50 floor. That floor broke in June 2026 at $16.60. Against a realistic $29-30 event-win value and a verified $16.50 floor, today's asymmetry is roughly 0.9 to 1, and we would be paying full probability-weighted value -- our base case is about $23 against a $22.94 price -- to own a supply shock.

The business deserves respect while we wait. Revenue grew 46% in the first quarter of 2026 and has now accelerated three quarters running; net dollar retention is 139%; free cash flow was $88.6 million on $333.4 million of revenue; the balance sheet carries about $1.58 billion of net cash and essentially no debt. The real reservation is not the artificial-intelligence headline but the gross margin behind it, which fell from 91.5% to 79.4% in a year as inference compute landed in cost of revenue -- a change management did not flag early. That is why the moat reads narrow and eroding, and why the value case is capped: a cheap revenue multiple on a structurally lower-margin base is worth less than it looks.

So: wait, with a named level and a named date. The flush is the 7 August 2026 release. If the shares trade at or below $18.50 in the two to three weeks after it -- ideally retesting the $16.60 June low and holding -- the asymmetry restores to roughly 5 to 1 against the same $29 target and this becomes a straightforward buy. If instead the release is absorbed and the stock breaks above $25 on volume with the remaining shorts covering, we will have missed a fast 20% and we should accept that rather than chase into a name whose only floor is sentiment. The wrong answer is the one in between: paying up for an event that adds supply before it removes an overhang.
interrogator_dossier:
# FIG (Figma, Inc.) — Forensic Dossier: Forced-Seller Special Situation

Event-driven review, re-verified live on 28 July 2026. The question in front of this committee is not whether Figma is a good business. It is whether the gap between today's price of about $22.94 and a plausible event-resolved value is wide enough to pay us, and whether the event that is supposed to close that gap is real, dated and binding.

Two findings drive this note. First, the catalyst is real and contractual, and the date is Friday 7 August 2026 — this confirms and re-sources the finding from the last pass, against an earlier review that could not locate the date and wrongly treated the event as open-ended. Second, and new to this pass, the positioning that was supposed to power the move has already begun to unwind: short interest has fallen from 78.2 million shares a month ago to 66.1 million now, while the stock rallied about 38% off its June low. The squeeze is being paid out before the event fires, and the buyer today is paying for it.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Figma listed on 31 July 2025 at $33, spiked to $142.92 on its first day, and has since fallen about 84% from that peak, bottoming at $16.60 in late June 2026. The first half of 2026 alone took roughly 52% off the shares. Since the June low the stock has recovered about 38%, closing at $22.94 on 27 July 2026 after an 8.6% single-day gain with no company news attached to it, and trading around $22.70 on 28 July.

The corporate story has changed shape over that year. At listing, Figma sold itself as the collaborative design canvas that Adobe had tried and failed to buy. Through 2026 the pitch has widened into an artificial-intelligence product-building platform: at its Config user conference on 24-25 June 2026 the company rebranded its workspace as an "intelligent canvas" for full-stack digital creation, and on 7 July 2026 it acquired the team behind Bud (formerly Orchids), an agent and code-generation tool. Pricing is shifting from pure per-seat toward a hybrid of seats plus usage credits, and management disclosed that roughly three-quarters of enterprise customers bought artificial-intelligence credits in the first quarter of 2026.

That is a genuine pivot, and it is being made under fire. Anthropic launched Claude Design at the end of April 2026, a directly competing design tool, and that single event is the proximate cause of most of this year's share-price damage. The market is no longer debating Figma's growth rate; it is debating whether seat-based design software survives at all.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers say |
| --- | --- |
| Growth is accelerating | Confirmed, from the filed statements. First-quarter 2026 revenue was $333.4 million against $228.2 million a year earlier, up 46.1%, and it followed 40% in the fourth quarter of 2025 and 38% in the third — three straight quarters of acceleration. Trailing-twelve-month revenue is $1.161 billion, up about 41%. Second-quarter guidance of $348-350 million was set above the roughly $330 million the street carried, and the full-year guide was raised by $55 million to $1.422-1.428 billion. |
| Customers are going deeper | Supported. Net dollar retention — how much a given group of existing customers spends this year versus last — climbed to 139% at 31 March 2026, a three-point sequential gain and the best reading in over two years. Customers spending over $10,000 a year grew about 37% to 15,218. That is direct evidence of switching costs. |
| The model is capital-light and cash-generative | Confirmed, and it is the strongest fact in the file. First-quarter free cash flow was $88.6 million on $333.4 million of revenue, a 27% margin; trailing free cash flow is about $239 million. The balance sheet holds $1.638 billion of cash and short-term investments against $56.2 million of total debt — roughly $1.58 billion of net cash, about $2.99 per share. There is no financing risk of any kind here. |
| The artificial-intelligence build-out is an opportunity, not a cost | This is where the story is richer than the trajectory justifies. Cost of revenue rose from $19.5 million to $68.7 million year over year — up 253% against 46% revenue growth — taking the reported gross margin from 91.5% to 79.4% in twelve months (about 82% on the company's adjusted basis). Inference compute is landing in the cost line, and management did not frame it for investors ahead of time. RBC downgraded to Sector Perform with a $22 target on precisely this point. |
| (Not claimed, but material) | The company lost $142.4 million in the first quarter on a generally-accepted-accounting-principles basis and about $1.40 billion over twelve months, the latter inflated by post-listing stock-compensation charges. Weighted average shares rose from 474.8 million to 523.5 million over the year, up 10.3% — roughly 10% new stock created annually. |

The honest summary: the demand story is true, the cash story is true, and the margin story is deteriorating faster than the narrative admits.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rising and offensive rather than defensive. Management is spending into the artificial-intelligence transition instead of trimming to protect margins, and raised the full-year revenue guide while doing it. The June conference announcements and the July acquisition are aggressive moves, not retrenchment. The tension is that confident spending, a twelve-point gross-margin decline and stock compensation at roughly half of revenue is exactly the combination an activist attacks — and one has: Findell Capital Management wrote publicly to the board on 28 May 2026 arguing the company is significantly undervalued and calling for cost discipline.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Medium-to-high on revenue, low on margin transparency. Four public quarters is a short record, but within it the company has beaten and raised: it cleared its own first-quarter range, guided the second quarter above the street, and lifted the year. There is no missed revenue guide to point at. Against that, a 91.5%-to-79.4% gross-margin path is the kind of change a credible team flags early, and this one did not. Reliability: Medium.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions dominate and none has a settled answer. Does artificial intelligence expand Figma's market or delete its seats? Where does gross margin settle once inference cost is fully loaded? When does stock-based compensation stop running near half of revenue? The covering analysts are split: fourteen firms carry an average target of about $30.40, with Citigroup at Buy and $35 (trimmed from $36 on 24 July 2026), Bank of America reinstated at Buy and $30 on 7 July 2026, Goldman Sachs at Buy and $30, and RBC at Sector Perform and $22 set on 25 June 2026. High target $38, low $22, no outright sells.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

Concerning:
- Gross margin down about twelve percentage points year over year, with cost of revenue up 253%.
- Stock compensation running near half of revenue, creating roughly 10% new shares annually — a permanent, self-renewing supply of stock that no lock-up expiry fixes.
- Only about 238 million of 528 million shares are in the tradable float today, and roughly 77.7 million more are contractually released in the first week of August 2026 — a one-third increase in tradable supply in a single step.
- Officers have sold steadily in the open market since May 2026 at prices from about $18.09 to $25.04, including the chief executive, chief financial officer, chief revenue officer, chief technology officer, general counsel and chief accounting officer. The most recent was the chief revenue officer on 14 July 2026 at $23.92. Several of these are pre-scheduled or tax-withholding disposals rather than discretionary bets, but the direction is uniform.
- Venture holders are distributing stock in kind to their limited partners, which is mechanical and price-blind. Index Ventures moved roughly 3.5 million shares out on 19 May 2026 and still holds about 53 million; Mamoon Hamid, a director and 10% owner, moved about 6.0 million out on 28 May 2026 and still holds 37.1 million. Those two alone control roughly 90 million shares.
- A dual-class structure with founder super-voting stock means outside shareholders cannot force change. The chief executive had to convert Class B stock into Class A merely to sell.
- New this pass, and the most important change: the short book is already covering. Short interest fell from 78.2 million shares to 66.1 million over the past month — now 27.75% of the float and 12.5% of shares outstanding, at 2.9 days to cover, down from the 35-42% of float that research desks were describing in mid-July. The squeeze that was supposed to be the reward for owning this into the expiry has been partly harvested by the 38% rally already.

Encouraging:
- About $1.58 billion of net cash, essentially no debt, and positive free cash flow through the entire decline. No covenant, no maturity, no dilution by necessity.
- Growth accelerating into the disruption rather than away from it, with 139% net dollar retention and a raised full-year guide.
- Consensus revenue of roughly $1.425 billion for 2026 and $1.761 billion for 2027 — the street has not written off demand.
- Three large banks turned constructive within a month (Citigroup on 1 July, Bank of America on 7 July, Goldman Sachs), all arguing artificial intelligence is a tailwind rather than an existential threat.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling shift is linguistic: the company now describes itself as a product-development platform rather than a design tool. That is a defensive widening — the ground under "design tool" is moving. interrogator_dossier:
# FIG (Figma, Inc.) — Forensic Dossier: Forced-Seller Special Situation

*Event-driven review. The thesis here is not business quality — it is the gap between today's
depressed price and where the stock can trade once a mechanical, calendar-driven wave of insider
selling finishes clearing. Verified live on the web as of June 29, 2026.*

## 1. THE SETUP IN ONE PARAGRAPH

Figma is the cloud design-software company that went public in late July 2025 at $33 a share, spiked
toward $140 in the first days of trading, and has since round-tripped all the way back — closing
around $16.84 on June 25, 2026 and trading near $18.68 intraday on June 29, down roughly 40% this
year and down close to 80% from the post-listing peak. The collapse is not, in the first instance, a
business story: revenue is $1.16 billion over the trailing twelve months and still growing about 41%,
the company holds roughly $1.6 billion of cash and marketable securities with little or no debt, and
it now generates real free cash flow ($88.6 million in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, a 27%
margin). What has crushed the stock is plumbing — a staggered "lock-up" schedule (the window during
which pre-IPO insiders are contractually barred from selling) that releases shares in waves and floods
the market with supply faster than new buyers arrive. The event we are underwriting is the clearing of
that overhang: the final and largest release falls on August 31, 2026, when holders of roughly 54.1%
of the Class A shares — venture funds and employees, about $7 billion of stock at current prices —
become free to sell. The bet is that once that last forced-seller wave washes through, the structural
discount it has carved into the price can begin to close.

## 2. IS THE CATALYST REAL, DATED, AND BINDING?

Yes on all three, and this is the strongest part of the case. The dates are not analyst guesses; they
come from the company's own contractual lock-up architecture, disclosed in SEC filings:

- A standard 180-day lock-up expired January 27, 2026.
- On August 30, 2025 Figma signed an *extended* lock-up covering ~54.1% of Class A shares, with
  staggered quarterly releases tied to earnings dates running through mid-2026 (unlock tranches landed
  around September 30 and December 31, 2025, and March 31, 2026).
- The final remainder — the venture-capital block holding over half the shares — releases on
  **August 31, 2026.**

So the forcing event is a hard, dated, contractual one. There is no FDA panel, no acquirer, no
regulator whose discretion could slip the date. That removes the single biggest risk in event
investing — an undated or serially-extended catalyst. The catalyst is binding because it is a calendar
mechanic, not a decision.

## 3. THE CRITICAL NUANCE — THIS IS A SUPPLY DUMP, NOT A RE-RATING TRIGGER

Here is the honest complication, and it is the thing the director must weigh hardest. A normal special
situation has a catalyst that *lifts* the price on a date (a deal closes, a drug is approved). This
one is the opposite: August 31 is the date the *largest wave of selling becomes legal*. The event
itself pushes the price down, or at best sideways under heavy volume, in the days and weeks around it.
The profit does not come from the unlock firing — it comes from the *absence of forced sellers* in the
weeks and months *after* the overhang has cleared, once the float has found permanent homes and the
mechanical seller is finally gone. In other words, the asymmetric entry is on the *far side* of the
wash-out, not in front of it. Every prior unlock tranche in this schedule (September, December, March)
"contributed materially to selling pressure and downward price movement." There is no reason to expect
the biggest tranche to behave differently.

## 4. THE VERIFIED DOWNSIDE FLOOR — AND WHY IT IS SOFT

The Catalyst-Watch board carries a floor of $17.50. The problem, verified today, is that the stock is
*already trading at or below that level* (≈$16.84 close, ≈$18.68 intraday). A floor the price has
already pierced is not a floor — it is a level the market has demonstrated it will trade through under
supply pressure. The real backstops are:

- **Cash:** ~$1.6 billion of net cash on ~528 million shares is roughly $3 a share. That is a hard
  asset floor but a low one — it does not protect $17.
- **A fundamentals-based floor:** one published discounted-cash-flow model pegs fair value near
  **$19.70** even on cautious assumptions, and the company is free-cash-flow positive and growing 40%+.
  That argues the *business* is worth roughly today's price or a little more — which means the downside
  from here is bounded more by valuation support (~$15–18 on a bad-tape, decel scenario) than by a
  contractual payout. There is no deal price, cash-tender, or recovery value that hard-caps the loss.

So the floor is real in the sense that a 40%-grower with positive cash flow and net cash will not go to
zero — but it is *soft*: it sits right where the stock already trades, and a heavy August unlock into a
weak tape could easily print $13–15 before it stabilizes.

## 5. RED FLAGS AND GREEN FLAGS

🔴 The biggest forced-seller wave is still *ahead* (Aug 31), so the supply pressure that has defined the
stock all year is not yet spent — buying now means standing in front of it.
🔴 The stated floor has already broken; downside is genuinely open below it on a bad unlock.
🔴 GAAP net loss of about -$1.40 billion over the trailing year (heavily stock-compensation and
IPO-driven) makes the headline screen look ugly and can keep generalist buyers away.
🔴 Sell-side conviction is *falling*, not rising — Wells Fargo cut its target from $42 to $36, RBC from
$28 to $22 — which weakens the "snap-back to consensus" leg of the bull case.

🟢 The catalyst is genuinely hard-dated and contractual — no slippage risk.
🟢 The underlying business is high-quality, not cheap-and-bad: ~41% revenue growth, positive free cash
flow at a 27% margin, ~$1.6 billion net cash, an AI product cycle (Config 2026 launches) that lifted
guidance.
🟢 An activist (Findell Capital) is now engaged, pushing cost discipline and focus — a second,
independent source of potential upside.
🟢 The math of the overhang is self-extinguishing: after August 31 there is no further contractual
seller. The single force depressing the price has a known expiry.

## 6. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT FOR THE DIRECTOR

The single most important thing to weigh: this is a real, hard-dated, binding catalyst — but it is a
forced-*selling* event, so the clean asymmetric entry is *after* August 31, 2026, not before it, and
the published floor has already been breached. The credible play is to wait for the final-unlock
wash-out to clear the decks, then buy the de-risked, supply-free name into a recovering business. Buying
in front of the largest unlock, below a floor that has already failed, is taking the supply risk for no
extra reward. Moat and secular-threat framing are largely beside the point on an event name like this —
the franchise is fine; the question is purely the supply mechanic and the entry timing.

# FIG — Figma Inc — Interrogator Dossier (Event-Driven Special Situation)

**Frame:** This is NOT a quality/compounding judgment. FIG is a forced-seller / post-IPO supply-overhang special situation. The thesis is the SPREAD between the live price (~$19.12, 06-22-2026) and an overhang-cleared re-rate target (~$32), gated on the final insider lock-up clearing, with a downside floor anchored to the post-washout technical base (~$16.60 52-wk low / ~$17.50 floor). The business is excellent (40%+ growth, design-software franchise); the price is wrecked by IPO mechanics, not by a broken franchise.

## 1. THE EVENT — is it real, dated, binding?

REAL and DATED, but the catalyst polarity is supply-RELEASE, not supply-CLEARING-by-a-fixed-trigger. Figma IPO'd late July 2025 (~$33 IPO, spiked to ~$142 intraday, then collapsed ~81% off the high; down ~40% YTD). On 2025-08-30 the company struck an Extended Lock-Up Agreement covering 54.1% of Class A shares (the VC/insider low-cost-basis block, >$6B notional) with a PHASED release: 17.5% (~38.9M) after Q3'25 earnings (DONE); 20% (~44.4M) after 2025 year-end earnings (DONE); 27.5% (~61.1M) after Q1'26 earnings (DONE); remaining ~35% (~77.7M) after Q2'26 earnings OR 2026-08-31, whichever FIRST. The load-bearing forcing function is the final ~77.7M-share unlock around the Q2'26 print / Aug 31, 2026 — a HARD, DATED, binding corporate event (SEC-filed 8-K). Critically, the event ADDS supply; it is bearish-on-arrival. The bull thesis is 'the LAST overhang tranche clears, the forced-seller is exhausted, and the float reprices to fundamentals' — a capitulation/washout setup, not a deal-close arb.

## 2. THE VERIFIED DOWNSIDE FLOOR

Technical/washout floor, not an asset floor. 52-wk low $16.60; dossier floor $17.50. Real support: $1.16B TTM revenue growing ~41% (Q1'26 +46% YoY, $333M), EV/S ~7x vs software peers ~19x. On any reasonable forward-sales multiple, ~$17-18 is a defensible base for a 40%-grower; the float would have to assume the entire insider block dumps at once AND a growth break for the floor to pierce. Real but a multiple-on-growth floor, not net-cash.

## 3. RED FLAGS (event-specific)

Catalyst polarity is wrong for an 'aggressive entry' — the dated event RELEASES >$6B of low-cost-basis stock; forced selling PRECEDES the re-rate. No deal/fixed payout/CVR/SoP gap — the $32 target is an analyst-multiple re-rate (street avg $36.88, range $25.25-$63), not an event-locked value. Massive net loss (-$1.40B, EPS -$3.38) keeps generalists away during the supply window. Dual-class founder control makes public float a price-taker to the insider selling cadence.

## 4. GREEN FLAGS

The worst of the overhang is mathematically already behind (65% of the locked block cleared Q3'25-Q1'26; Aug'26 is the LAST tranche). Franchise intact and reaccelerating (+46% YoY Q1'26). EV/S 7x vs peers ~19x is a genuine post-washout discount on top-decile-growth SaaS. Live ~$19.12 sits only ~9% above the $17.50 floor — downside tightly bounded and largely realized.

## 5. CATALYST CLASSIFICATION

Dated (Aug 31, 2026 / Q2'26) and binding, but a supply-RELEASE that must be ABSORBED before the re-rate, with upside an analyst-multiple re-rate rather than a contractual payout. SOFT_EXTENDED / capitulation-watchlist, not a clean PENDING_HARD arb. Right posture: WAIT FOR THE FLUSH (the Aug unlock), then enter on a confirmed exhaustion base.

## 6. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Classify: PIVOTING (post-IPO repricing, franchise intact). The single most important thing the director must weigh: this is a forced-seller exhaustion trade whose load-bearing event ADDS supply on a fixed date — you are paid to wait for the Aug'26 unlock to flush, not to front-run it. Floor real (~$17.50), downside bounded (~9%), but the catalyst is bearish-on-arrival, so the asymmetry is a WATCHLIST (B), not an aggressive entry (A). Moat: NARROW design-collaboration franchise (network/switching costs); secular AI design-tool displacement is manageable, not terminal, since Figma is itself shipping AI features.
